extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining when and how U.S. patents, U.S. patent application publications, certain international (PCT) application publications, and related documents are available and may be used as prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e), including how to determine the relevant reference date and how to overcome rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant date = critical date for foreign patents (102(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: The critical date of a foreign patent as a reference under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d) is the date the patent becomes enforceable (issued, sealed or granted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the foreign patent is kept secret after grant (e.g., sealed), the grant/issue/seal date is the relevant date for 102(d) rejections; case examples include In re Monks and related decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrecy after grant does not negate 102(d) effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A period of secrecy after granting the patent (as in some countries) has no effect on the use of the foreign patent as prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents kept secret at the patentee's option have been held usable in rejections under 102(d) as of the grant date (e.g., Gramme Elec. Co. and In re Talbott). Such secrecy may, however, affect applicability under other subsections (e.g., 102(a)/(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Same invention requirement for 102(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d), the 'invention... patented' in the foreign country must be the same as the invention sought to be patented in the U.S.; the foreign application must support the subject matter of the U.S. claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims need not be identical or in the same statutory class; if the foreign specification fully discloses the invention and thereby supports U.S. claiming options, 102(d) applies to disclosed aspects even if the foreign claims are narrower or different (In re Kathawala).

rubrics_metrics.name: Which documents qualify as prior art under pre-AIA 102(e)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) allows use of certain U.S. patents, certain U.S. patent application publications, and certain international application publications as prior art as of their respective U.S. filing dates (including certain international filing dates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must determine whether the reference qualifies under the statute and whether its earliest effective U.S. filing date (or applicable international filing date meeting criteria) is appropriate; see MPEP §706.02(a) for examination guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: SIRs treated as U.S. patents (eligible as prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Published Statutory Invention Registrations (SIRs) will be treated the same as a U.S. patent for defensive purposes and are usable as references as of their filing date under 35 U.S.C. 102, including pre-AIA 102(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §1111 for SIR details; a published SIR is prior art as of its filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defensive publications are prior art only as of publication date
rubrics_metrics.description: A defensive publication is not an application publication under 35 U.S.C. 122(b); it is a publication and therefore is prior art only as of its publication date, not its filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Defensive Publication Program (April 1968–May 1985) produced abstracts that are prior art only from publication (Ex parte Osmond). See MPEP §711.06(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of U.S. application as reference when no common assignee/inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is no common assignee or inventor, a U.S. application must issue as a patent or be published as a SIR or as an application publication before it is available as prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only issued patents, published SIRs, or application publications meeting statutory criteria are usable as prior art absent common ownership; see MPEP §706.02(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional rejections allowed for copending applications with common inventive entity
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is a common assignee or inventor, an examiner may make a provisional pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection over an earlier-filed, unpublished copending U.S. application (i.e., before that prior application publishes or issues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional rejections put applicant on notice and allow more options to overcome the rejection; they are authorized only where there is a common inventor or assignee. See Ex parte Bartfeld and MPEP §706.02(f)(2)/(k).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on provisional rejections after statutory amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: For applications filed on or after November 29, 1999 or pending on or after December 10, 2004, a provisional 103(a) rejection using prior art under pre-AIA 102(e) is not proper if the application contains evidence that the application and the prior art reference were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person at the time the invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See changes effected by the Intellectual Property and High Technology Technical Amendments Act of 2002 and relevant MPEP sections (§706.02(l)(1)-(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: CREATE Act may disqualify non-commonly owned references for 103
rubrics_metrics.description: The CREATE Act (2004) can cause certain non-commonly owned references to be treated as commonly owned for purposes of determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103(c) if statutory conditions are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CREATE Act applies only to subject matter qualifying as prior art under 102(e),(f), or (g) and relied upon in a 103 rejection; it does not disqualify references under 102(a)/(b) or affect double patenting rejections. See MPEP §706.02(l).

rubrics_metrics.name: Entire disclosure of patent/publication may be relied on under 102(e)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 102(e) rejection may rely on any part of the disclosure of a U.S. patent, U.S. patent application publication, or qualifying international application publication having an earlier effective U.S. filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of any disclosed embodiment, example, or teaching in the reference is permitted (Sun Studs, Inc. v. ATA Equip. Leasing). See MPEP §706.02(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference must itself contain the subject matter relied upon
rubrics_metrics.description: When relying on a U.S. patent or application publication under pre-AIA 102(e), the disclosure used in the rejection must be present in the issued patent or application publication itself; canceled portions or material omitted from the issued/publication are not available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subject matter disclosed only in an abandoned/unpublished parent or canceled in prosecution cannot be used to antedate under 102(e) (Ex parte Stalego, In re Klesper, In re Lund). See MPEP §901.02 for abandoned app availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional application benefit requires 112 support
rubrics_metrics.description: A U.S. patent that claims benefit to a provisional application is usable as prior art under pre-AIA 102(e) as of the provisional filing date only if at least one claim of the patent is supported by the provisional application's disclosure in compliance with pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §706.02(f)(1) and examples; inadequate provisional support prevents the provisional filing date from being the critical 102(e) date (see Dynamic Drinkware v. National Graphics).

rubrics_metrics.name: International (PCT) filing date treated as U.S. filing date only if three conditions met
rubrics_metrics.description: An international (PCT) filing date is a U.S. filing date for prior art purposes under pre-AIA 102(e) only if (1) the international filing date is on or after November 29, 2000, (2) the international application designated the United States, and (3) it was published by WIPO under PCT Article 21(2) in English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If all three conditions are met, the international filing date (or an earlier proper benefit date) may be used as the 102(e) reference date, provided the relied-upon subject matter is supported in the earlier application in compliance with 112. If not met, treat the reference under 102(a)/(b) as of publication or under 102(e) as of a later U.S. filing date where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of international applications filed before Nov 29, 2000
rubrics_metrics.description: International applications filed prior to November 29, 2000 are subject to the pre-AIPA version of 102(e); various specific rules apply depending on whether the reference is a U.S. patent, U.S. application publication, or WIPO publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example: (1) U.S. patents: apply 102(e) as of earlier of completion of 371(c) requirements or filing date of later U.S. application claiming the international app; (2) U.S. and WIPO publications: generally not applied as 102(e) as of publication date under the older statute but may be used under 102(a)/(b); (3) follow the three listed subrules in MPEP §2136.03(B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefit of nonprovisional parent (35 U.S.C. 120) requires 112 support
rubrics_metrics.description: A U.S. patent or application publication that claims benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 to an earlier nonprovisional (continuation/divisional/CIP) is accorded the earlier filing date as its 102(e) prior art date only if the earlier-filed application properly supports the subject matter relied upon in the rejection in compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a)/pre-AIA 112, first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subject matter not supported in the earlier application cannot be given the earlier date. See MPEP §706.02(f)(1) and examples 2 and 5–9.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference date is filing date, not conception or reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: For pre-AIA 102(e) references, the effective prior art date is the filing date in the U.S. (including certain international filing dates); the date of conception or reduction to practice of the reference inventor is not relevant unless 102(g) interference issues arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (e.g., Sun Studs v. ATA; related decisions) confirm that disclosed earlier inventive activity in a reference does not antedate the filing date absent evidence of actual earlier reduction to practice in this country when 102(g) applies. See MPEP §2138 for related topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different inventive entity = reference is 'by another'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Another' in 102(e) means other than applicant(s); if there is any difference in inventive entity (not all inventors are the same), the reference is considered 'by another.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even shared inventors are immaterial; a reference with even some different inventors is prima facie evidence the invention was made 'by another' (In re Land; Ex parte DesOrmeaux). See MPEP §2136.04 and §706.02(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods to overcome a pre-AIA 102(e) rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A 102(e) rejection can be overcome by antedating the filing date of the reference (e.g., via an affidavit/declaration under 37 C.F.R. 1.131) or by showing that the disclosure relied on describes an inventor's or at least one joint inventor's own work (via 37 C.F.R. 1.132), or by establishing entitlement to an earlier priority/benefit date that properly supports the relied-upon subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 1.131 to antedate where appropriate; use 1.132 when the reference describes the applicant's or joint inventor's own work. Earlier foreign priority or provisional dates may antedate the reference only if they meet statutory requirements and provide 112-compliant support. A terminal disclaimer does not overcome a pre-AIA 102(e) rejection. See MPEP §706.02(b), §715, §2136.05 and cited cases (In re Mathews, In re Gosteli, In re Costello, In re Bartfeld).

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing a reference describes the inventor's own work
rubrics_metrics.description: To overcome a prima facie 102(e) case where the reference names a different inventive entity, applicant may show the disclosure describes the inventor's or at least one joint inventor's own previous work by evidence such as association (same assignee), direct or indirect communication of the invention to the patent-application inventors, or other proof of derivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proving association/derivation can rebut the presumption that a reference by different inventive entities is 'by another' (In re Mathews, In re Whittle, In re DeBaun, In re Land). The facts of cooperative research, shared labs, cross-references, or common preparation may support or defeat the rejection depending on the record.
